why_how.text: Mirror setup and head checks clear your own blind spots, and you stay out of other drivers' blind spots.
Pedestrians and other vulnerable users are protected by specific yield and stop rules.

scenario.text: Gil approaches a crosswalk where a person with a white cane is crossing.

reasoning.text: You come to a full stop for cane or guide-dog users and for any pedestrian lawfully crossing.

result.text: Gil comes to a full stop and waits until the person has crossed.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking slowing down is enough when a cane user is crossing.

correction.text: The manual requires a full stop for cane or guide-dog users and any lawful crossing, and failing to stop and causing serious injury or death brings a Class one misdemeanor.

memory_support.text: Cane, dog or lawful crossing: full stop.

prompt.text: A person with a guide dog is crossing in front of Gil. Is slowing enough?

answer.text: No. Gil must come to a full stop.

rationale.text: Cane, guide-dog and lawful crossings demand full stops backed by a Class one misdemeanor.

lines.text: Your blind spots.
Other drivers' blind spots.
Vulnerable road users.

narration.text: Welcome to the first lesson on sharing the road. We start with blind spots: how to set your mirrors, how to check the areas mirrors miss, and what to do when you are riding in someone else's blind spot. Then we turn to vulnerable road users. The manual lists who they are and says that distracted or careless driving around them is illegal, and that you must drive to cover their mistakes. Finally we cover the rules for pedestrians: guarding them near schools, playgrounds and homes, letting them fully cross before you turn, and the full stop required for cane or guide-dog users and any pedestrian lawfully crossing.

lines.text: Inside mirror: frame the whole back window.
Side mirrors: barely show your vehicle.
Head turn and shoulder glance before moving.

narration.text: Set the inside mirror to frame the whole back window. Set the side mirrors so that they barely show your own vehicle. Then clear your blind spots with a quick head turn and a shoulder glance before lane changes and passes. And never linger in another driver's blind spot: speed up or drop back instead. Put as a contrast: your own blind spots need mirror setup plus head checks, while others' blind spots need you to speed up or drop back out. The mirrors are a starting point, and the head turn finishes the job before you move. Both halves of the rule, mirrors and the shoulder glance, are part of every lane change.

lines.text: Pedestrians, bicyclists, wheelchair, skateboard, skate, scooter users.
Animals and animal-drawn vehicles.
Careless driving around them is illegal.

narration.text: Vulnerable road users include pedestrians, bicyclists, and wheelchair, skateboard, skate and scooter users, as well as animals and animal-drawn vehicles. Distracted or careless driving around them is illegal, and you must drive to cover their mistakes. That last phrase means you drive in a way that leaves room for their mistakes, not only your own. Guard pedestrians near schools, playgrounds and homes. Let them fully cross before you turn. Never pass at a crosswalk, and stop and stay stopped until pedestrians clear your stopped lane. The next slide covers when a full stop is always required.

title.text: A full stop, not a slowdown

lines.text: Cane or guide-dog users: full stop.
Any pedestrian lawfully crossing: full stop.
Failing and causing serious injury: Class one misdemeanor.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver sees a pedestrian crossing and simply slows down, rolling through behind them. For certain crossings the manual requires more. Come to a full stop for cane or guide-dog users, and for any pedestrian lawfully crossing. Failing to stop and causing serious injury or death brings a Class one misdemeanor. Put as a contrast: turning drivers wait out full crossings, while cane, guide-dog and lawful crossings demand full stops backed by a Class one misdemeanor. So when a cane or guide-dog user is crossing, or any pedestrian is lawfully crossing in front of you, slowing is not enough. Stop fully, and wait until they have crossed.

lines.text: Guide-dog user crossing.
Slow down or stop?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a person with a guide dog is crossing the street in front of Gil. Is it enough for Gil to slow down and let them pass? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Gil must come to a full stop. You come to a full stop for cane or guide-dog users and for any pedestrian lawfully crossing, and failing to stop and causing serious injury or death brings a Class one misdemeanor. Gil also needs to let the person fully cross before he turns, and to stay stopped until they clear his stopped lane. The memory line is short: cane, dog or lawful crossing means a full stop, every time.

lines.text: Mirrors plus a head turn.
Speed up or drop back out of blind spots.
Full stop for cane, dog or lawful crossings.

narration.text: To close the lesson: set the inside mirror to frame the whole back window and the side mirrors to barely show your vehicle, and clear blind spots with a head turn and shoulder glance before lane changes and passes. Never linger in another driver's blind spot; speed up or drop back. Vulnerable road users include pedestrians, bicyclists, wheelchair, skateboard, skate and scooter users, animals and animal-drawn vehicles, and you must drive to cover their mistakes. Let pedestrians fully cross before you turn, never pass at a crosswalk, and come to a full stop for cane or guide-dog users and any pedestrian lawfully crossing.

why_how.text: Bicyclists share the road with clear rights, and drivers owe them specific room.
Bicycles and motorcycles are easy to miss, so they need checks, double looks and extra following distance.

scenario.text: Jo comes up behind a bicyclist in a lane too narrow to pass with room to spare.

reasoning.text: Pass cyclists with at least three feet of clearance, changing lanes where the lane cannot spare it.

result.text: Jo changes lanes to pass, keeping at least three feet from the cyclist, and never enters the bike lane.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a driver may use an empty bike lane to pass slower traffic.

correction.text: Motor vehicles may never use marked bike lanes, even to pass.

memory_support.text: Three feet for bikes; look twice for motorcycles.

prompt.text: Jo wants to pass a cyclist. How much room must she give?

answer.text: At least three feet, changing lanes if the lane cannot spare it.

rationale.text: Drivers owe cyclists three feet, lane changes where needed, and empty bike lanes.

lines.text: Bicyclist rights.
Passing and bike lanes.
Motorcycles: look twice.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on sharing the road with bicycles and motorcycles. Bicyclists have the same right-of-way as motor vehicles, with some specific rules about where they ride. Drivers owe them a set amount of passing room and must keep out of bike lanes. Bicycles can slip into blind spots, so the manual lists the moments to check for them. Motorcycles are easy to overlook, so the manual asks for a second look and more following distance. By the end of this lesson you should know the three-foot passing rule, the bike lane rule, the moments to check for bicycles, and the extra second behind a motorcycle.

lines.text: Share motor-vehicle right-of-way.
May hold the lane center when needed.
All public roads except interstates and most freeways.

narration.text: Bicyclists share motor-vehicle right-of-way. They may hold the center of the lane when needed for left turns or in narrow lanes. They may ride on all public roads except interstates and most freeways. And on sidewalks, paths and two-way bike lanes, they may approach from either direction. So a bicyclist in the middle of the lane is not breaking a rule when the lane is narrow or a left turn is coming. Expect cyclists on almost every public road you drive, and expect them from either direction on shared paths and two-way bike lanes. These rights set up the duties drivers owe them, which come on the next slide.

lines.text: Pass with at least three feet of clearance.
Change lanes if the lane cannot spare it.
Never use a marked bike lane, even to pass.

narration.text: Pass cyclists with at least three feet of clearance. Where the lane cannot spare that much room, change lanes to pass. Motor vehicles may never use marked bike lanes, even to pass. Put together: bicyclists may take the lane center and most roads, while drivers owe them three feet, lane changes and empty bike lanes. So if you cannot give three feet within your lane, the rule is to change lanes, not to squeeze by. And a bike lane is never a passing lane for a car, even when it is empty. Learn the three-foot number together with the ban on driving in a marked bike lane.

lines.text: Bikes slip into blind spots.
Check before pull-outs, lane changes, turns, backing, doors, intersections.
Give room; expect sudden stops.

narration.text: Bicycles slip easily into blind spots. Check for them before pull-outs, lane changes, turns, backing, door openings and intersections. Give them room, and expect sudden stops. That list of moments is worth memorizing, and opening a car door is on it. Compare motorcycles: bikes need checks at these maneuver points because they slip into blind spots, while motorcycles need double looks because drivers expect four-wheelers. For motorcycles, the manual also says to check blind spots before every maneuver. And look twice for motorcycles, since drivers expect four-wheelers and miss motorcycles until too late in over half of car-motorcycle crashes.

lines.text: Drivers expect four-wheelers.
Bikes missed until too late in over half of car-motorcycle crashes.
Never tailgate or lane-share; add a second.

narration.text: Here is the trap. A driver glances, sees no car, and pulls out in front of a motorcycle. The manual says look twice for motorcycles, since drivers expect four-wheelers and miss motorcycles until too late in over half of car-motorcycle crashes. Check blind spots before every maneuver. Never tailgate or lane-share with a motorcycle. Add an extra second of following distance, and double it in bad weather. Expect sudden moves within the lane, and yield with double looks, since a motorcycle's speed and distance can deceive you. So motorcycles gain an extra following second, doubled in bad weather, plus bans on tailgating and lane sharing.

lines.text: Cyclist ahead in a narrow lane.
How much room?
May you use the bike lane?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Jo comes up behind a bicyclist in a lane too narrow to pass with room to spare. How much room must she give, and may she use the marked bike lane to get around? Work it out before reading on. The answer: at least three feet of clearance, changing lanes where the lane cannot spare it, and no, she may never use a marked bike lane, even to pass. Jo changes lanes when it is safe and passes with at least three feet between her car and the cyclist. Drivers owe cyclists three feet, lane changes where needed, and empty bike lanes. Three feet for bikes; look twice for motorcycles.

lines.text: Bicyclists share right-of-way.
Three feet; never the bike lane.
Motorcycles: double look, extra second.

narration.text: To close the lesson: bicyclists share motor-vehicle right-of-way, may hold the lane center when needed, and ride all public roads except interstates and most freeways. Pass them with at least three feet of clearance, change lanes if the lane cannot spare it, and never use a marked bike lane, even to pass. Check for bicycles before pull-outs, lane changes, turns, backing, door openings and intersections. Look twice for motorcycles, never tailgate or lane-share with one, and add an extra second of following distance, doubled in bad weather. The memory line: three feet for bikes, and look twice for motorcycles.

why_how.text: Norfolk's light rail, The Tide, crosses roads at many points, and the manual sets clear rules for driving near it.
Low-speed vehicles have speed and road limits, and golf carts are not low-speed vehicles.

scenario.text: Ana drives toward a light rail crossing in Norfolk, and traffic ahead is backed up across the tracks.

reasoning.text: Never stop on the tracks, and cross only with room to clear fully.

result.text: Ana waits before the tracks until there is room for her car to clear them fully.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a golf cart counts as a low-speed vehicle.

correction.text: Low-speed vehicles run twenty-one to twenty-five on roads of thirty-five or less, while golf carts are not low-speed vehicles at all.

memory_support.text: Never stop on the tracks; golf carts do not count.

prompt.text: Traffic is backed up across the light rail tracks ahead of Ana. Should she pull onto the tracks to wait?

answer.text: No. She never stops on the tracks and crosses only with room to clear fully.

rationale.text: Light rail forbids stopping on tracks and demands full clearance before crossing.

lines.text: Norfolk light rail, The Tide.
Low-speed vehicles.
Golf carts.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on light rail and low-speed vehicles. In Norfolk, the light rail line called The Tide has twenty-seven crossings over seven point four miles, and the manual sets out how to drive near it. Then we look at low-speed vehicles: how fast they go, which roads they may use, who may drive them, and what rules they must meet. We will also settle one common question, which is whether a golf cart counts as a low-speed vehicle. Both topics come with short lists of rules, and the key to each is a pair of contrasts: what light rail forbids and what it demands, and what low-speed vehicles are compared with golf carts.

lines.text: Trains on any track at any time.
Never circle lowered gates or stop on tracks.
Look both ways; cross only with room to clear.

narration.text: Around Norfolk light rail, The Tide, with twenty-seven crossings over seven point four miles, expect trains on any track at any time. Never circle lowered gates, and never stop, pass or shift lanes on the tracks. Look both ways before turning across the tracks, and cross only with room to clear fully. Put as a contrast: light rail forbids circling gates and stopping on tracks, while demanding train expectation, double looks and full clearance. So at a light rail crossing, you never stop on the tracks, and you start across only with room to clear fully.

title.text: Golf carts are not low-speed vehicles

lines.text: Low-speed vehicles: twenty-one to twenty-five miles per hour.
Only on roads posted thirty-five or less.
Golf carts do not qualify.

narration.text: Here is the trap: a golf cart is not a low-speed vehicle. Low-speed vehicles top out at twenty-one to twenty-five miles per hour and may run only on roads posted thirty-five miles per hour or less. They may be driven by licensed drivers or supervised permit holders, and they must meet federal safety rules plus Virginia registration and insurance rules. Golf carts do not qualify. So low-speed vehicles run twenty-one to twenty-five on roads of thirty-five or less, while golf carts are not low-speed vehicles at all. If an exam question asks whether a golf cart counts, the answer is no, and the low-speed vehicle rules do not cover it.

lines.text: Licensed drivers or supervised permit holders.
Federal safety rules.
Virginia registration and insurance.

narration.text: The rules for low-speed vehicles cover the vehicle, the road and the driver. The vehicle tops out at twenty-one to twenty-five miles per hour and must meet federal safety rules plus Virginia registration and insurance rules. The road must be posted at thirty-five miles per hour or less. The driver must be a licensed driver or a supervised permit holder. Put those three parts together and you have the full rule. On a road posted thirty-five or less, a low-speed vehicle you meet may be traveling at twenty-one to twenty-five miles per hour.

lines.text: Traffic backed up past the tracks.
Pull onto the tracks to wait?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Ana is driving toward a light rail crossing in Norfolk, and traffic ahead is backed up across the tracks. Should she pull onto the tracks and wait there for traffic to move? Work it out before reading on. The answer is no. Around The Tide, you never stop on the tracks, and you cross only with room to clear fully. Ana waits before the tracks until there is room for her whole car to clear them. She also expects trains on any track at any time, looks both ways before turning across, and never circles lowered gates. Never stop on the tracks is the rule to remember.

lines.text: Trains any time, any track.
Never stop on the tracks.
Golf carts do not count.

narration.text: To close the lesson: around Norfolk light rail, The Tide, with twenty-seven crossings over seven point four miles, expect trains on any track at any time. Never circle lowered gates, and never stop, pass or shift on the tracks. Look both ways before turning across, and cross only with room to clear fully. Low-speed vehicles top out at twenty-one to twenty-five miles per hour, may run only on roads posted thirty-five or less, must be driven by licensed drivers or supervised permit holders, and must meet federal safety plus Virginia registration and insurance rules. Golf carts do not qualify. Never stop on the tracks, and golf carts do not count.

why_how.text: Large vehicles are longer, higher and wider, accelerate slowly and need long distances to stop and turn.
Their side, rear and front No-Zones each hide you or trap you in a different way.

scenario.text: Dan has just passed a tractor-trailer on the highway.

reasoning.text: Return only with the whole truck front in your mirror, and hold your speed.

result.text: Dan waits until he can see the whole front of the truck in his mirror, then moves over and keeps his speed.

claim.text: Common mistake: cutting back in right after passing a truck and then slowing down.

correction.text: Front No-Zones punish cutting in too soon or slowing after passing, since trucks need nearly twice car stopping time and room.

memory_support.text: No face in the mirror, no view of you.

prompt.text: Dan has just passed a truck. When may he move back into its lane?

answer.text: When the whole front of the truck shows in his mirror, holding his speed.

rationale.text: Passing returns need the whole truck front in the mirror at steady speed, because front No-Zones punish early cut-ins.

lines.text: Longer, higher, wider.
Side, rear and front No-Zones.
Wide turns and trailers.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on sharing the road with trucks, buses and RVs. Trucks, tractor-trailers, buses and RVs are longer, higher and wider than cars. They accelerate slowly, and they need long distances to stop and turn. Their danger areas are called No-Zones, on the sides, the front and the rear. In this lesson we take each No-Zone in turn, then look at how large vehicles turn and what you must never do beside a turning truck, and finally at towing light and medium trailers. Each rule in this lesson comes back to the No-Zones and to the extra room large vehicles need.

lines.text: Side No-Zones dwarf car blind spots.
No face in the mirror: the driver cannot see you.
Rear No-Zone: no escape at sudden stops.

narration.text: Side No-Zones on trucks, buses and RVs dwarf car blind spots, because of their wide turns. If you cannot see the driver's face in his mirror, he cannot see you. Rear No-Zones hide your car from the truck driver and hide the traffic ahead from you, leaving no escape at sudden stops, so always hold a safe following distance. Put together: side zones hide you beside wide-turning trucks, and rear zones hide you behind sudden stoppers. The mirror test is a simple check you can use on every large vehicle you drive near: look for the driver's face in the mirror, and if you cannot see it, assume the driver cannot see you either.

lines.text: Do not cut in too soon or slow after passing.
Trucks need nearly twice car stopping time and room.
Return only with the whole truck front in your mirror.

narration.text: Here is the trap. After passing a truck, a driver cuts back in quickly and then slows down. The front No-Zone punishes exactly that, because trucks need nearly twice the stopping time and room of a car. Combinations can run up to sixty-five feet and may need over half a mile to pass. So return only when the whole front of the truck shows in your mirror, and hold your speed. Front zones punish early cut-ins, and passing returns need the whole truck front in the mirror at steady speed. If you slow down right after cutting in front of a truck, you take away the room it needs to stop.

lines.text: Trucks, buses and RVs swing wide to turn.
Blind spots up to twenty feet ahead and about two hundred feet behind.
Never squeeze between them and the curb.

narration.text: Trucks, buses and RVs swing wide to turn. Their blind spots reach up to twenty feet ahead of the cab and about two hundred feet behind. Never squeeze between them and the curb, or between them and another vehicle. Put as a contrast: passing returns need the whole truck front in the mirror at steady speed, while turning trucks forbid squeezing past at all. So when a truck ahead of you swings wide, the space it leaves beside the curb is not an opening for your car. Stay back and let it complete the turn. Remember the two blind spot distances as a pair: up to twenty feet in front of the cab, and about two hundred feet behind.

lines.text: Light and medium trailers: safety chains, hitches, large mirrors.
Towing doubles passing, stopping, accelerating, turning effort.
No-Zones apply.

narration.text: Light and medium trailers ride on safety chains and hitches, and large mirrors are needed. Towing doubles the effort of passing, stopping, accelerating and turning, and No-Zones apply to a vehicle towing a trailer too. Put as a comparison: trailers double every maneuver's effort, matching the near-double stopping demand of trucks. So if you tow a trailer, the effort of passing, stopping, accelerating and turning doubles, and No-Zones apply to your vehicle and trailer. Plan every maneuver with that doubled effort in mind, and use the large mirrors the manual says a trailer needs.

lines.text: You have passed a truck.
When may you move back?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: Dan has just passed a tractor-trailer on the highway. When may he move back into the truck's lane? Work it out before reading on. The answer is when the whole front of the truck shows in his mirror, and he should hold his speed as he moves over. The front No-Zone punishes cutting in too soon or slowing after passing, because trucks need nearly twice car stopping time and room. Combinations can run up to sixty-five feet, so passing one takes time and room. No face in the mirror means no view of you, and no whole truck front in the mirror means it is too soon to move back.

lines.text: Side: watch for the driver's face.
Rear: keep a safe following distance.
Front: return only with the whole truck in view.

narration.text: To close the section: trucks, buses and RVs are longer, higher and wider, accelerate slowly and need long distances to stop and turn, and their danger areas are called No-Zones. Side No-Zones dwarf car blind spots, and if you cannot see the driver's face in his mirror, he cannot see you. Rear No-Zones leave no escape at sudden stops, so hold a safe following distance. After passing, return only with the whole truck front in your mirror, and hold your speed. Never squeeze between a turning truck and the curb. Towing a trailer doubles passing, stopping, accelerating and turning effort, and No-Zones apply to trailers too.
